utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you ready to proceed or continue with Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 30 which is the book by General Kadijevic, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a problem with my computer system; could this be solved if possible, because I can highlight parts of the transcript, but I have not the right file on it now so if this could be .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is this the CaseView method that we have which is not coming through?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is the CaseView on the small computer; I can work with it instead of just looking at it. It can be done easily within a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you like to continue, please, with Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. DR. JAMES GOW, recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you please look at page 77 of Exhibit 30 for me, please? Is there a reference in the book by General Kadijevic there to this question of the JNA fulfilling its objectives in the campaign in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. If your Honours recall, I was indicating yesterday that the JNA, in my judgment, had begun possibly with the objective ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you turn on your microphone, please, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was turned on. I do not know why it has gone off. If your Honours recall, I was saying at the end of yesterday that, in my judgment, the JNA could well have begun the period of the war of dissolution after June 1991 with the objective of holding together the SFRY and of not going to war. That is a question about which I do not think anybody can be clear. Some people say it, clearly, had the ambition of war at that stage and before; my judgment would be that it probably did not quite. Following that, as we saw through excerpts from General Kadijevic yesterday, it formulated a programme for action in Croatia that would go in two phases. The more extensive objective would be to topple the government in Zagreb and to take control of Croatia. The fall back objective, which was the first phase of operations, was to establish the borders around -- of a new entity around Serbian dominated, majority Serbian population, areas or areas which were deemed to be necessary to be part of the territories being controlled and in which there might be minority Serbian populations. In attempting to achieve that lesser objective, which was what I have referred to as a new political project, that is, the project to create the borders of a new entity, a new set of territories which would be a mini Yugoslavia, what in some circles has been described as a set of federated Serbian states, and that the borders -- and that there would be specific borders for this new entity incorporating parts of Croatia and parts, if not possibly in some cases the whole, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the section that I will just indicate here, you will see that General Kadijevic notes that in close co-ordination with the Serb insurgents, that is, the Serbian irregular forces in Croatia, all the Serb regions, i.e. those designated as being part of the objective of the first phase, and that is what I would judge to be the fall back objective, the borders for this mini Yugoslav state, were achieved except a part in western Slavonia. I think the fact that he indicates "except for a part in western Slavonia" all the territories they sought to take control of, in their terms to liberate, the fact that he indicates that they did not achieve something is a clear indication that they had a specific idea of what the boundaries of that mini Yugoslavia would be in this case, although I cannot tell you exactly what the boundary in western Slovenia would be because the General does not indicate what it would be either. I would supplement this by saying that also General Panic, to whom we made reference yesterday, who at the time we are talking about was commander of the First Military District and was later to be Chief of Staff of the JNA, has also indicated the same thing, that they were unable to achieve all their objectives in western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what were the consequences for Bosnia following the activities of the JNA in Croatia in the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was put in a difficult situation as this evolved. I think I already made mention yesterday of the problems that were beginning to develop at the intercommunal level. At the state level, Bosnia was obviously in a weaker position than, for example, Slovenia or Croatia might have been, although Croatia was, of course, in a weaker position than Slovenia had been, in this process of disintegration of the SFRY. The pressures of the war in Croatia meant that the JNA began to mobilize and use parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina for actions in Croatia, and at the same time began a series of manoeuvres and exercises to mobilize Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina into the reserve units of the JNA into certain parts of the Territorial Defence structure (whilst not mobilising non-Serbian people in other areas, and, in some cases, seeking to disestablish Territorial Defence forces in majority Muslim or Croat areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think General Kadijevic also makes reference to this, does he not, in pages 78 and 80 of the Exhibit you have there with you, Exhibit 30 -- perhaps it is 80. Page 80.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe you can highlight this section so that we can see it. You see that in the section I indicate, you see the section I indicate, that the General reinforces what I was just saying; during the war in Croatia, the JNA manoeuvred and used troops via Bosnia and Herzegovina which was to be of vital significance for the JNA. This was both in the war in Croatia, but also, as he goes on to say, the manoeuvres and movements, which were not without problems, also enabled the mobilization of Serb parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be very successful. So this was already creating part of the framework for possible later operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the General indicates here that after leaving Croatia that they should have a strong JNA force in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This, I would suggest, a part of the whole process of mobilisation, is because the General regarded the situation, the position, of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina as being the backbone of any future communist state for the Serbian people. If you will permit me a moment, I think I may find this here as well, but if you wish to press on, I can provide you with relevant references later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will move on, Dr. Gow. Parallel with the activities of the JNA in Bosnia, was there any corresponding political developments that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1991, the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia, the SDS, declared four autonomous regions between this 12th and 19th September. These were declared as Serbian autonomous regions, first in Eastern Herzegovina, later of the Bosnian Krajina of north eastern Bosnia, sometimes known as Semberija and of Sarajevo-Romanija. These were later to be supplemented in November by the declaration of a fifth autonomous region of northern Bosnia. Indeed, in January 1996, for a period there was a brief semi-declaration of the further autonomous region as a break-away from the Sarajevo- Romanija district, but this seems not to have been fully implemented. This process was the creation of the territorial and for the shadow political infrastructure, I would say, for the borders of the Serbian territories to be designated as part of the mini Yugoslavia, to which I made reference following from General Kadijevic, in Bosnia and Herzegovina and, therefore, included large parts of north western Bosnia and northern Bosnia, north eastern Bosnia, eastern Bosnia and the very south western part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, known as eastern Herzegovina. This would leave parts of western Herzegovina in some areas in central Bosnia, presumably, not to be part of this entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you look at the document you are now shown? Can you tell us what the document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a page taken, one page, yes, from a Montenegrin publication, Monitor, which has taken an extract from a Belgrade publication, Vreme, and makes reference to a tape which was produced by the last Federal Prime Minister of the SFRY, Ante Markovic. It was a tape which Markovic produced at one of the later meetings of the Federal government while it was still trying to sit in September 1991. It reports -- it indicates that the tape that Markovic had, indicates, according to the text, a conversation between Slobodan Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic in which Milosevic is reported to be saying to Karadzic that he should get in touch with General Uzelac, Commander of the Banja Luka corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps before we go into that, I will tender it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 45?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 45 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be marked and then handed back? Perhaps you might display it on the screen and then go through it, Dr. Gow. Is that the part that refers to that conversation, Dr. Gow, you referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you see is the first page of the English translation of the Serbo-Croat text which is provided. It makes reference in the first line to something called "plan RAM". This is something about which there has been much discussion since this period and, indeed, slightly before it, across the territories of the former Yugoslavia. The existence of the plan is not, as far as I am aware, confirmed but many people have talked about it. On the other hand, some people have denied its existence. The purported purpose of this plan, to which on the tape reference is made, was for preparations and execution of the creation of this set of territories throughout parts of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina based around the Serbian -- based around the Serbian populations there, and around areas of which they would to take control. If we can move on, on to the second page, you see an extract from the conversation reported in which Milosevic tells Karadzic: "Go talk to Uzelac, he'll tell you everything" ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Who is this "Uzelac"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, when I think I probably was not supposed to be speaking, I had already begun to say General Uzelac was Commander of the Banja Luka corps of the JNA. The implication is that as you read through this that Uzelac would be helping the SDS leader by distributing weaponry and giving other forms of logistical existence, I would surmise. The reported conversation indicates the possible existence of such a plan and certainly, if it is accepted, indicates the co-operation between the SDS and the JNA in making these preparations in Bosnia and Herzegovina in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, I would ask you to look at this document that I show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I just point out -- would you mind if I pointed to one more thing on this, which is at the very end, just there is one small section in which the then Federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, indicates that it is his judgment that the voices are undoubtedly those of Milosevic and Karadzic, giving an indication that Karadzic should contact Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what is the document I have just given you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a transcript of the tape of the conversation between Slobodan Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic, and indicates that the conversation took place on 29th May 1991. This is a transcript of the tape to which the previous article we looked at made reference, the tape that was produced by the Federal Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is a full transcript of that conversation, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I would ask for the audio tape to be actually played, but while it is being -- perhaps I should do this first, I will tender that transcript now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there an objection to Exhibit 46, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have a problem here. That is the reason why we are objecting to it. There is no source where that tape is coming from. There is a difference here if we look into Exhibit 45 because there it is a newspaper that is a source -- be it true or not, that is not the issue here -- but here we have a blank tape without anything.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will not proceed with this Exhibit just for the moment, if your Honours please. I will pass on it and come back to it, I think. So perhaps that document could be returned to us. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, was the JNA being prepared for military activity in Bosnia during the latter part of 1991 and the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was. The JNA was being prepared for military activity through this -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One minute, Dr. Gow. What is the problem, Mr. Tadic, can you hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He could not hear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can you hear me now in your language? Can you hear me now? Are you able to hear me in your language? THE ACCUSED TADIC: (Responds affirmatively in Serbo-Croat, not interpreted).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, your Honour. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, was the JNA being prepared for military activity in Bosnia during the latter part of 1991 and the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA was carrying out a series of exercises and manoeuvres on territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina, moving military forces through the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some of these were clearly in relation to the war in Croatia, others, I would suggest, were in preparation for possible future needs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time, the exercises and manoeuvres were being used as a mechanism for mobilizing elements of the Serbian population into armed forces, structures, in the Territorial Defence and in the JNA reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were any concerns raised in Bosnia about these preparations by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Questions were asked in the Bosnian Parliament in September in which it was asked of the JNA what its activity in Bosnia at that time was intended for. Concerns were being expressed at the way in which the JNA was on the road throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What measures were taken to strengthen the JNA and the Serbian position in Bosnia in the late part of 1991 and the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The manoeuvres and exercises, to which I have already made reference, were being conducted and at the same time the JNA appears to have begun a process in some areas of moving its troops mostly out of garrisons so that they would probably not face the same situation that they had in Croatia where they were trapped in garrisons as the conflict began.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At this stage, I would ask you to go to page 50 of Exhibit 30, Dr. Gow, in the book by General Kadijevic, please. If it could be placed on the screen? In relation to preparations by the JNA, is there a reference there or a segment there that you can take us to concerning that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the section, in the sentence here, the General indicates the importance of using the Territorial Defence structures in Serb regions in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina in co-operation with the JNA for realising that this concept of deployment for the operations which were being undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You see a reference there, "Accordingly, all Territorial Defence units were disarmed prior to the outbreak of fighting", do you know when that occurred approximately in terms of dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence Forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina were being disarmed through the latter part of 1991 -- in some areas were being disarmed through the latter part of 1991 and in conjunction with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also into the first part of 1992, this was joint activity between the JNA and parts of the Bosnian government. These efforts on the part of the Bosnian government were said to be as a means for trying to avoid the potential for conflict, to try to take away, to co-operate with the JNA and try to make sure there was no conditions for conflict. At the same time, it is my understanding that the JNA was ostensibly taking the weapons away for them to be renewed, and there was some suggestion that they would be renewed at a future date. It appears that in Serbian areas this process of disarmament was not taking place and, in fact, some of the arms were being redistributed into those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Redistributed to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Redistributed to Territorial Defence Forces in Serbian majority areas in which the majority Serbian population, or elements of the majority Serbian population, were being mobilized into the Territorial Defence Force through the exercises which were being carried out in conjunction with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that I now show you?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, Dr. Gow, that last sentence that begins, "Naturally, we used the Territorial Defence of Serb regions in Croatia", "Territorial Defence" means Territorial Defence Forces, I gather; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That document that you see there, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy taken from the Belgrade publication, Yugoslav Survey, and it is an extract concerning the platform of the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina and organisation of the Yugoslav community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who obtained the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you consider this to be a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender this document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to, I believe that is, Exhibit 47?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 47 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just looking at that document, can you take us to the relevant portion that you wish to refer us to in connection with your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the date on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The original document is, I believe, from 21st October. I had better check -- sorry, 16th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the significance of this in terms of your evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall that a short time ago I described the creation of the four Serbian autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the proclamation of them, in September 1991. Partly in response to this, in October 1991, the Bosnian Parliament held a session to discuss the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its position within the obviously difficult situation as the SFRY was disintegrating and as there was a war going on in Croatia. At that time, you will see by reference to paragraph 2 of the document, that the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that stage affirmed the sovereign state quality of Bosnia and Herzegovina, indicating them to be a state of equal citizens and peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the Muslims, the Slav Muslims, the Serbs and the Croats, as well as any other population groups living on the territories. This was a significant assertion of the sovereign statehood of Bosnia as one of the elements of the SFRY; if you move on to paragraph 3, I think you can take the reference to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina being integral and indivisible as being a reference, as being in reference to the declaration of the Serbian autonomous regions, that is, to make it clear that the declaration of Serbian autonomous regions and the growing suspicion that there would be an attempt to change the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina either by force or if, as could be expected, it were not to be achieved any other way, and therefore the Parliament was making a comment. I should point out that a large number of the Serbian Democratic Party representatives at this stage did not participate in the vote because they did not wish to recognise the vote that was being taken, which I would say again is an indication in support of their -- I would say again was an indication of the intention which was emerging in the declaration of the Serbian autonomous regions to try to create the borders of a new entity which would challenge the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Bosnian state as defined in the 1974 constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, this is linked to what you said a moment ago about the JNA manoeuvres and so forth on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, what I am indicating is that the political activity of the SDS in this context, the military activity of JNA units on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, indicated, gave sufficient grounds for many people to wonder whether what was going to happen, and to suspect the intention of trying to create a territorial expansion of the Republic of Serbia, or of the rump Yugoslavia, depending on which terminology is used, through the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. This appeared to be what was underway in Croatia, as I think General Kadijevic's book indicates was the case, and it was what was suspected to be the case in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a mark of the way in which the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Parliament with a Muslim Croat majority regarded the situation and wanted to reassert the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina in opposition to the declarations of the autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this concern that was happening in Yugoslavia at this stage, not only in relation to Bosnia but generally, reflected in the international community as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In connection with that, would you look at the next document I show you, please? (Handed) Can you tell me what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is an extract taken from the volume "Yugoslavia Through Documents" edited by Snezana Trifunovska to which reference has been made in my testimony already. The particular extract refers to a declaration on the situation in Yugoslavia adopted at an informal meeting of the Council of Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the European Communities and its Member States.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you regard that as a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 48?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 48 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that could be displayed on the projector? Do you see there the expression of concern by in this case the European Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicate for the benefit of your Honours that the date of the statement was 6th October 1991. I would also draw your attention to the reference to agreements reached at The Hague on 4th October 1991 between the Presidents of Croatia and Serbia and General Kadijevic. The context for this was the European Community Conference on Yugoslavia which was organised from September 1991 through to the summer of 1992. That conference, as part of the EC's concern for the situation in Yugoslavia, attempted to seek an overall solution to the conflict and dispute on territories of the SFRY. The significance of this, if I may move to the second page -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have a question. The passage that I see on my screen is concerned certainly with heavy fighting in Yugoslavia. It does not seem to be concerned with preparations by the JNA in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought it was that that was giving rise to concern in Europe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The concern in the EC and among its Member States at this stage was for the situation in the territories of the SFRY as a whole -- I do not understand why my microphone keeps suddenly going off ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mine keeps doing it too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you are touching it by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I am not touching mine.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will check it at the recess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- there was concern for the situation on the territories of the SFRY as a whole where it was clear that there was a major political dispute between the various republics which had constituted the SFRY, and at the moment this declaration was made there was clearly a significant armed conflict taking place on the territory of Croatia. There was no specific reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina in this document. But if I may move on to the second page, I can explain the significance of this document with reference to the previous document ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that the significant aspect of the meeting on 4th October was that the solution that was to be sought would be in the perspective of the recognition of the independence of those republics which were seeking it. This was a recognition which was made in principle by the Serbian President at the meeting on 4th October, that the republics would be given recognition of the sovereignty of the republics and, therefore, the right of the republics to independence. This was an agreement which Serbia was later to withdraw on 18th October, but from this point onwards, and the significance of the agreement is that the concession was made in principle on 4th October, and that from this point onwards the EC addressed the problems of the conflict in respect of the right to independence of the republics seeking it. With reference to the previous document affirming the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina in October, you will note that that declaration of sovereignty would also fit into the context of the discussions taking place in The Hague concerning the sovereignty and possible independence of those republics seeking it on the basis of their sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Following on from that, did the European Community then proceed to set out the basis upon which new states in Eastern Europe would be recognised and, in particular, Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, in the course of October, the European Community Conference drafted a document, a draft Convention, on arrangements between the Yugoslav states. That agreement was drafted on the basis of the agreement, in principle, of President Milosevic on 4th October. On 18th October, when the document was presented, President Milosevic rejected the document. In that context, the EC then said that if there was not agreement to this document within the space of a month, then on the basis of its statement of this day and of a meeting that occurred at the same time and on the basis, I think, of the principle agreement on 4th October, it would proceed towards recognising the independence, the possibility of recognising the independence, of those republics seeking it on the basis of the state sovereignty as expressed and discussed at the EC conference. When Serbia did not agree to the draft convention in November 1991, the EC then began to move towards recognising the independence on the basis of these discussions and these documents. On 16th/17th December 1991, the EC set out guidelines for the possible recognition of independence of new states emerging from the communist Federations in the Soviet Union, in Czechoslovakia but, particularly, in the case of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that is now shown to you, please? (Handed). Is this the guidelines that you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy, this a document again taken -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I am told that only five microphones can work at once. You’ve had three on in front of you at one point. I know you move around a lot and that is a problem, but keep it to one, perhaps two. You have two and I guess if I turn mine on we are at maximum, so you keep one on, Mr. Niemann, and you just need one, I do believe, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I need two because whenever I use one you cannot hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am told to turn three on because nobody can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is because you move around so much. You are going to have to stand somehow or, perhaps, we may have to get a microphone to clip on you. Try with your one and you may use two and I will turn mine off. The technical booth tells us that it is better for you to use one, Dr. Gow. We can hear you pretty well; if we cannot, we will let you know that we cannot hear you. So will you operate with one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am happy to operate with one. I just found it frustrating yesterday constantly to be told that I could not be heard, but I am happy with one if that is agreeable.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We heard pretty well. You have one. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): The document that you have before you, you just were telling us, that is that declaration that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document I have before me is an extract from the Trifunovska volume, edited volume Yugoslavia Through Documents, to which reference has been made a number of times. The extract is the EC declaration concerning the conditions for recognition of new states adopted at the Extraordinary European Political Counsel Meeting, Ministerial Meeting -- sorry, European Political Co-operation Ministerial Meeting on 16th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be tendered, if your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 49?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour, without any technical sound.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Although you have to speak into yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 49 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just looking at that particular exhibit, could you take us to the principal conditions that were set down with respect to recognition of states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first indicates that the declaration invited those Yugoslav republics wishing to be recognised as having independence in time for the meeting on 15th January indicated there, should indicate this to the European Community and its Member States by 23rd December, and that in doing so they should wish that they wish to be recognised as having independent international personality and that they accept the commitments outlined in the guidelines. The guidelines themselves -- if I can try to move it down -- are mentioned in a footnote to the text. If we can move on to the second page -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps go back, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have not finished reading the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Go back to that page. The next page, would you go on to that now, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The footnote continues on to the following page in which the guidelines for recognition themselves are identified, including recognition of relevant international treaties and political agreements. If your Honours have had time to read the guidelines, I would also indicate finally that the Community and its Member States made it clear that they were not prepared to recognise any entities which were the result of an act, what they deemed as an act, of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a consequence of these conditions being set out, did Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, respond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The presidency and government of Bosnia and Herzegovina made an application to the EC and its Member States for recognition as having independent international personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the Bosnian-Serb response to the actions taken by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs did not -- the Bosnian Serb, in this case I talk about the adherence of the SDS and its supporters -- the Bosnian Serbs in this case, as defined, did not support the application of the presidency and government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as could be expected through the decisions of the Assembly which they had formed and through the declaration of the Serbian autonomous regions, and on 9th January they designated a constitution which would come into effect and create a Serbian republic of the people of -- a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina comprising the territories of the autonomous regions in the event of Bosnia and Herzegovina being recognised as having independent international personality. They asserted that this territory would be a part of Federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there a name that is commonly applied to this republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name at this stage was the Serbian Republic of -- the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the course of 1992, the name of this entity was changed to Republika Srpska, a name by which commonly it is referred, a name by which reference to it is commonly made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the next document that I show you? (Handed) What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a copy of an extract from the official gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is dated 27th January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does it appear in Serbian with a translation into English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the English translation of the document obtained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the English translation was provided by Dr. Radomir Lukic from the designated Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 51?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 50. Any objection to 50?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 50 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): I think that the declaration can be seen, can it not, on the English translation on about the fourth page of the English document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure your Honours can read, but I will just indicate for convenience the title is the Declaration on the Proclamation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It indicates in Article 1 that the territories of the Serbian autonomous areas or regions would comprise the territories of those areas as well as areas in which it is said that Serbian people were removed by a process of murder and expulsion during the Second World War. It indicates in Article 2 that this Republic is intended to remain part of the federal state of Yugoslavia, and be a federal unit of that state. This would be consistent with the kind of project I was identifying earlier in the writings of General Kadijevic, to create a mini Yugoslavia comprising parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, later to become the Republic of Srpska, then proceed to draw up its own constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look now at the document which I show you? (Handed) Firstly, can you tell us what the document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is again a copy of the Sluzbeni glasnik, the official gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date on it is 16th March. It refers to the decision on the proclamation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that decision is from 28th February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 51?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 51 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Perhaps you might just show us at least the front page of the English translation of that document? Dr. Gow, does that refer at the top of the document the date 16th March, but then in the preamble the reference to the decision of 28th February 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any other part of the document you wish to go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we could move to the following page, you will note in the basic provisions of the constitutional document that, "The Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, state of the Serb people and of all citizens living therein", I think this is an indication that there was the possibility that any people who were prepared to remain part -- non-Serbian people who were prepared to remain part of this entity could have a place in it. I may make further reference to that later in testimony. The article 2 again indicates in the constitution that the territory of this Republic will consist of the Serb autonomous regions, municipalities, etc. and so forth, as in the article I referred to in the January 9th declaration. Again it states that the Republic is a part of the Federal state of Yugoslavia. So, indicating again that it would be a federal unit linked with Serbia and Montenegro rather than a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might move to the final page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stay there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One question. The capital of this territory was Pale or Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The territory was not Knin. As far as I recall, the capital was not designated. At the time of this activity, Banja Luka in north western Bosnia appeared to be the de facto capital. This is where many of the discussions in Assembly meetings were taking place. I think later the capital de facto became Pale. I am not in a position to say categorically that the capital was Banja Luka, Pale or, indeed, anywhere else -- maybe I should be but I am afraid I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it was not Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not Knin; Knin was within a territory designated as the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Croatia which would be a separate unit within this set of federal structures and, if I may say, would clearly be the capital of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that Exhibit be returned then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I wish to go to the final page. If I may just finally draw your attention to Article 144 which indicates that this provisional constitution will come into effect on the day of its proclamation, and the date of proclamation was to be 7th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A moment ago in your evidence, Dr. Gow, you referred to the fact that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had actually applied for recognition by the European Community.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the response then of the European Community to this application?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The European Council of the Member States in taking this course of action asked an Arbitration Commission, which had been established as part of the European Community Conference on Yugoslavia, to advise on the guidelines which had been established. That Arbitration Commission was under the presidency of Monsieur Robert Badinter who was President of the French constitutional court. In the case of each of the four applications which were made by the former Yugoslav republics seeking independence it offered an opinion. The four republics seeking independence were Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia. In the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Arbitration Commission in its opinion indicated that, although the presidency and government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had made the declaration of independent -- sorry, had sought independence on the basis of the parliamentary vote in October 1991, when we saw the document I referred to as the platform on the sovereignty of Bosnia in the context of the Yugoslav community, that although that had taken place, the fact that the Serbian Democratic Party had declared autonomous regions, and that the Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party had indicated that it did not support that platform, meant that there should be a -- that the position in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not clearly established at this time. It advised, among other things, that clarification possibly might be found through the holding of a referendum under international supervision

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In connection with the answer you have just given to my question, would you please look at the document that is now shown to you? (Handed) Dr. Gow, what is this document that you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a copy of Opinion No. 4 by the Arbitration Commission on international recognition of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the European Community and its Member States. The document is from 11th January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, yes, thank you, your Honour, it is 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is exhibit ---

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- no objection. Exhibit 52 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Just looking at this particular Opinion, consisting of three pages, is there any particular part that you would take us to in connection with what you have already said in terms of the conditions that were to be set for recognition, or the suggestion, perhaps, might be a better way of putting it? I think I direct you to the very last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following what I was just saying, you will see in the paragraph here that the Commission chaired by Monsieur Badinter noted that outside the institutional framework of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 10th November, the Serbian people had voted for the common Yugoslav state and indicated that it did not support this position, and that through to 9th January they had proclaimed the independence of this Serbian Republic, one of the documents we saw a few moments ago. I then move through and indicate that, as you read from paragraph 4, the Commission thought that in these circumstances the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state cannot be held to have been fully established. Because of this assessment, it goes on to suggest that clarification is needed possibly by means of a referendum of all the citizens and to be carried out under international supervision. That is, in fact, what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The referendum was conducted on 29th February and 1st March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the European Arbitration Commission on the international conference on former Yugoslavia then address the matter following that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following the holding of the referendum, the Arbitration Commission was then asked, was again asked to express an opinion. In its opinion it judged that a referendum had been held under international supervision and that two-thirds of those voting had voted for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that, therefore, this was sufficient to constitute an expression -- sufficient to express sufficiently the will of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The EC and its Member States and other countries then proceeded to recognise the independent international personality of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately the percentage of voters that participated in this referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The percentage of the voters was, I think, 63 and a half per cent; of those something over 90 per cent voted for the independence of the Republic, therefore, satisfying the condition established by the Parliament that any move to independence -- as I recall it, any move to independence would require a two-thirds vote of the population -- sorry, of those voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look please at the document that I now show you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, this was despite the fact that the Bosnian Serbs had boycotted the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in spite of the fact that large numbers of Bosnian Serbs had either boycotted or been prevented from taking part in the referendum. That is the case. One reason why only 63.5, or thereabouts, per cent of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina participated in the referendum was that large number, large parts of the Serbian communities in Bosnia were not participating in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This document that I now show you, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of an Opinion No. 8 by the Arbitration Commission and relates to -- it is actually going to be very difficult to read -- the opinion, it relates to the opinions on the independence of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was this document obtained from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was obtained from the European Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 53?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 53 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, do you wish to take us to any particular part of that document? I think on the final page there is a reference to the consequences of the referendum and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will see that the Arbitration Commission notes that, "the referendum proposed in Opinion No. 4 was held in Bosnia and Herzegovina on 29th February and 1st March and that a large majority of the population voted in favour of the republic's independence". That relates overall to the question on the dissolution of the SFRY, indicating that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was regarded as having independent international personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is the data of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date of the document ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it is on the bottom of the page that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I think was 4th July 1992. Yes, it was 4th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, but in terms of recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had there been some steps taken by the international community prior to this date of 4th July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document itself acknowledges that a large number of states in the international community of states had recognised the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 7th April 1992, the European Community and its Member States recognised the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as did the United States; many other countries followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you look for me, please, at the next document that I show you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could just also confirm, beyond the recognition of other Member States, as can be seen on the document here, on 22nd May 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina, along with two other former Yugoslav states which had been recognised, was admitted to membership of the United Nations; again a further confirmation of its participation as an independent international actor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the international conference on the former Yugoslavia's Arbitration Commission then express an opinion in which it stated, in its view, when the various republics had seceded from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Arbitration Commission was asked by the international conference on the former Yugoslavia -- this was the successor conference to the European Community conference established jointly by the European Union and by the United Nations -- the Arbitration Commission was asked to clarify an earlier opinion. In its Opinion, I think, No. 1 of November 1991, it had indicated that the SFRY was in a process of dissolution. It was asked to confirm if that process of dissolution had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document that I now show you? (Handed) What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a copy of Opinion No. 11 of the Arbitration Commission responding to a question put by the co-chairman of the steering committee of the conference on Yugoslavia on 20th April 1993. The date of the opinion itself is 16th July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 54?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 54 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you hand it back? If you could take us to the relevant provisions of that opinion but, in particular, I think paragraphs 6 and 10 on pages 2 and 3 respectively.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will see that in the opinion of the Arbitration Commission relating to opinion No. 4 of 11th January 1992, to which reference has already been made, the Arbitration Commission judged that the referendum had been held, that a majority of the people expressed themselves in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and that the referendum was officially promulgated on 6th March, that is, the result was announced and the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Itzebegovic, declared independence. The Arbitration Commission then makes the judgment that since that date, notwithstanding dramatic events that have occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the constitutional authorities of the Republic have acted like those of a sovereign state in order to maintain its territorial integrity and their full and exclusive powers. So, 6th March 1992 has become, must be considered, the date on which Bosnia-Herzegovina succeeded the SFRY. That is the date on which it became independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think further down the page at paragraph 10 they summarise their views in respect of all of the republics, do they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in answer to the question as a whole, in paragraph 10, the Arbitration Commission expresses its view that the dates on which the states emerging from the SFRY can be regarded as having left the SFRY and have become independent are 8 October 1991 for Croatia and Slovenia; 17 November 1991 for the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia; 6 March 1992 for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, finally, 27 April 1992 for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro. That would be the date on which there could be no longer any question of the continuing existence of the SFRY, although it seems doubtful that anybody would say it continued to exist before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, a moment ago you said in your evidence that states had begun the process of recognition of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as early as 6th April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may correct you, I said 7th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry. Would you look at the document that you are now shown, please? (Handed) What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an extract taken from the Trifunovska volume "Yugoslavia through Documents" to which reference had already been made. The particular extract concerns the declaration on the recognition of Yugoslav republics by the EC, in particular, the EC declaration on recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and President Bush's statement on the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Slovenia. The dates to which I made reference are 10th March 1992 for the declaration on recognition of Yugoslav republics, the 6th April for the EC declaration and 7th April for President Bush's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 55. Is that the declaration itself, the EC declaration, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 55 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. (To the witness): Can you just point to those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I point, first of all, to item No. 173 in the Trifunovska volume, you will see it is the EC declaration on recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is dated 6th April 1992. It indicates that the community and its Member States decision to recognise as of 7th April 1992 the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Immediately underneath that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately, if I move down the page you will see a statement by President Bush of the United States of America made in Washington on 7th April 1992 indicating that United States recognises Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as some of the other Yugoslav, former Yugoslav republics as sovereign and independent states.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what was the reaction in Banja Luka of the Bosnian Serbs to the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated earlier that on 7th April 1992 the Bosnian Serb political movement indicated -- declared implementation of the February 28th provisional constitution and that took place in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This document that I now show you, does that relate to the answer you have just given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a copy of the official gazette of the Republika Srpska and contains the constitution of the Republika Srpska. The date for the official gazette is 31st December 1992 and the date for the constitution is 17th December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 56?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 56 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, what was the effect or purpose of this document in relation to the constitutional development of the Republic of Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first way in which this document is significant is because it indicates the change in name from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Republika Srpska. If I could move to the first Article of the constitution, you will note that in the provisional constitution of 28th February, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the state of Serbian people and other people and the citizens of the state. In this case, the Republika Srpska is the state of the Serb people alone, no mention of others, of other possibilities. But you will note that the territories used to constitute the Serb ethnic entities, that is, what were the autonomous regions, it establishes the borders only by means of a plebiscite. I am not clear that that plebiscite was ever taken, although a series of plebiscites were taken on a number questions. Finally, it again confirms in December 1992 that the Republic is part or regards itself as part of Federal Yugoslavia and, therefore, not part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that exhibit could be marked and returned? Dr. Gow, going back, if we may, to April 1992, following the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what then followed this process of international recognition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Leading up to and following the international acknowledgment of Bosnia and Herzegovina's independent international personality, there was a major armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you just look at this map that I now show you? (Handed) Dr. Gow, what does this map relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map indicates places in the early part of the period we are discussing in March and April 1992 in which armed conflict occurred in the very first weeks of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The map is slightly stylized and indicates major communication points in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who prepared the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor at my direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Exhibit 57?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 57 will be admitted. Before you get into a discussion of that, Mr. Niemann, we will take a recess for 20 minutes. We have received, Mr. Wladimiroff, the motion on Defence access to the accused. Have you received a copy of that, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then we will consider that after the recess when we return. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, we have received the motion on Defence access to the accused. I have reviewed it. Would you wish to state your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I think a little to add to what has been written in the motion by itself; I take it it is self-explanatory, so you will understand what is the argument. The argument is simply based on the general principle which is recognised in most jurisdictions, that the Defence has free access to the client and, therefore, it should not be limited otherwise other than, for example, official observations, but not by numbers or other restraints. If I may add, we have asked for the Trial Chamber to order that a Defence counsel and their designated consultant be allowed free access. May I add to that that we also wish you to set the conditions because so far we have only been able to discuss matters with our client here in these premises while the door was open and the guards were able to overhear what we were discussing. We would rather prefer not to be heard. So, therefore, we ask that you set conditions under which we may talk to our client, not overheard by the guards.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have attached to the motion, Mr. Wladimiroff, a letter to you dated May 8th 1996. It says: "Professor Wladimiroff, the Registrar has considered your request that two of your expert witnesses be allowed to meet Mr. Tadic in the holding cell at the Tribunal for the purposes of consultation". Then it says: "I regret to inform you that such an arrangement is not possible since the cells at the Tribunal are not suitable for conferences of several people. For this reason, the Registrar has confined visits at the Tribunal to the detainee's legal representatives. It will, of course, remain possible for the expert witnesses to visit Mr. Tadic at the detention unit. I apologise for the inconvenience which this may cause. Signed by Dominique Marro, the Deputy Registrar". With respect to your first request, the access, I think I will ask Mr. Marro to respond, if he wishes. This is the letter that he submitted to you. It sets forth his reasons. That was not the decision of the Trial Chamber. It was the decision of the Registrar. So let me hear from Mr. Marro.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I draw your attention before you ask Mr. Marro to respond to No. 6 of the motion, because I think that is a relevant part as far as the restraints are concerned here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. What you say is that since the Defence has visited the accused of the Tribunal with four persons at several previous occasions, this restraint seems unfounded where the Defence requested for the access of four persons today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marro?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point I wanted to make was that the Registry has always tried, as far as possible, to help out the Defence as well as any other people involved in this trial, so there is no principal objection to the request being made. Now, the problem here is mainly that of a practical nature, because in part of this building there are five small cells which have been set up in such a way that accused are, in fact, waiting there before they appear at the trial. For any possible discussion to take place, this has not actually been provided for. I do regret that because the confidential nature of the discussions has not been secured. I would personally be in favour of having a possibility for those who want to discuss in those cells to do so, these discussions being confidential. But, for security reasons and for reasons of convenience, of course, allow visits in these cells. Clearly enough, we have always allowed the counsels of the accused to be able to pay visit to their clients and to take the necessary instructions from them, because of the hearings taking place. Now, the problems we were faced with yesterday and, contrary to the point explained by Mr. Wladimiroff, were not members of the Defence. We are not talking about attorneys and counsel with a power of attorney. We are talking about witnesses. Of course, they are experts but they are witnesses. We thought that the dividing line between the attorney and witnesses would not enable us to secure free access under such conditions. I would also add to that that over and above the concerns expressed by Mr. Wladimiroff yesterday afternoon, we are trying to look for another possible way of settling this problem; in other words, having discussions between the experts and the accused. I do hope that we will be able to use another room in forthcoming weeks. It might not be available at all times, but at least it will enable us to settle the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It seemed to me that we have two questions. One has to do with the cell itself, with the number of cells. There may be some problem with the privacy, so to speak, of Mr. Tadic's discussions. But if you have met with four persons, but the door, I gather, has been opened, so you would want to meet and the door would be closed, is that not so, along with the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there a problem with from that for security purposes, Mr. Marro?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do hope and I do think that if this is being instructed to us by the judges, we will certainly meet that request, but I do not think that witnesses should find themselves in the accused's cells. It would not be a right thing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not asking for witnesses; you are asking for an expert witness, I gather. He is a witness but a different kind of witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Beside that, it had not been noticed to the Registrar that these gentlemen are expert witnesses, are at this stage of the trial consultants.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The person who wanted to speak with Mr. Tadic is at counsel table, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We want to speak with Mr. Tadic in their presence and discuss reactions from Mr. Tadic in their presence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is the gentleman who is sitting at counsel table, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And another gentleman sitting in the audience hall.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Both of whom will be expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: They may be expert witnesses; so far they are consultants to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They are consultants but they may be designated as expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The reason I am asking you is that it seems to me that there is a difference between expert witnesses and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. We are not going to present any witness of fact to Mr. Tadic and discuss matters with him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, without talking with the head of the security -- we have only heard from the Registrar -- we will allow, at least until we have had an opportunity to confer with the chief of security, expert witnesses to confer with Mr. Tadic along with the lawyers, but there will be a maximum of four persons at any one time in the cell in this building with Mr. Tadic. So that may be on occasion two persons who you may designate at some point in the trial as your expert witnesses along with two lawyers, but in any case, whatever combination, no more than four persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is exactly what we wanted so we are very pleased.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, and the door may be closed when you are conferring with him. As I indicated, we will talk with the chief of security. If there are any problems with that, then we will advise you and, if necessary, we will enter an order. At the present time, we do not have that problem because only one cell is being occupied in this building at this time. There may come a time, though, when that will not be the case and perhaps an adjustment will have to be made. Also, as Mr. Marro indicated, there is a room that will be adjacent to this courtroom where possibly arrangements can be made where you will have a little more comfort in your conferring. We will advise you of that as the days go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We appreciate that. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, there is just one matter I wish to clear up before we proceed to look at the last exhibit that you were given which arose earlier in testimony. You said in relation to the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina that there was a 63 per cent participation, but a number of people of Serbian nationality did not participate in this vote because they were prevented from doing so. Can you just assist us, perhaps, by going a little further and telling us who it is that you were referring to, so far as you know, that prevented them from participating in this referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think his testimony was that there was a certain number that did not participate either because they chose not to or were prevented, but you will talk now, I gather, about that proportion who were prevented, according to your understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that in some areas people were prevented from, or attempts were made to prevent people (and in cases successful attempts) from participating should they have decided to do so because the elements of the SDS and, according to reports, in conjunction with elements of the JNA created barricades which prevented ballot boxes being taken into certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just to conclude that, you were not in making reference to people of Muslim nationality or of Croatian nationality as preventing these people from voting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not indicating that political or official representatives of either of those communities was attempting to do that. I would not be a position to say whether or not any individual member involved in such activity was or was not of any particular ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Going to the map which has now been made Exhibit 57 and in relation to the war that followed in Bosnia-Herzegovina following the recognition of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's state, can you refer to that map in terms of the military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map as displayed indicates the main communications axes through Bosnia and Herzegovina. It indicates the dates on which violent armed incidents connected with the war occurred. These were not only following the international acknowledgment of the independent international personality of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also in the period immediately prior to it. The first of these clashes was at Bosanski Brod on 27th March, and at the same time there were clashes at Derventa, which should actually be -- the star should actually be on the communication axis there rather than halfway along. There were also incidents at places, for example, such as Bijeljina on 2nd April, that is, in the period prior to the international acknowledgment of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 7th April, and also at Kupres here. The nature of these incidents which continued after the international recognition and were to take place at all the other places designated in this first month of attack appear to be part of a co-ordinated Serbian JNA programme of activity to establish a framework of control for all the access and communication points into and out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You will note that all the places where there were these incidents in the first month of the war are all places of points which control completely access into and out of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are on the main communications axes, so you will see the early action of Bosanski Brod was particularly with reference to the possibility and, indeed at that stage, the reality of Croatian army forces being in place on the border there. All the incidents take place either at entry points into Bosnia and Herzegovina or at points of major importance on the communications axes, that is, in a manner so as to prevent, by taking control of those areas -- in a manner so that by taking control of those areas access could either be guaranteed from Serbia and Montenegro into Bosnia and Herzegovina to support the campaign, or could be denied to anybody wishing to try to give assistance from the territory of the Republic of Croatia. The incidents were accompanied by a series of actions involving JNA and paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at this document that I now show you? (Handed) Dr. Gow, what does that map represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a map representing control of territory by the different armed forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would say, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who prepared the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor at my direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection to 58; it will be admitted on your exhibit list, Mr. Niemann. You indicate that it is areas of control in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Should it be 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am just going to ask that question, your Honour. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, I think you just said then, and for the transcript, 1993; do you mean 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said 1993. I would be prepared to accept that it was for 1992. The situation changed relatively little in much of this period. The reason why I said 1993 is because of the extent of the green on the map and it looks more like 1993.
