I asked for the map to be drawn up and I will accept that if this was on the basis of information for 1992, that is what it indicates. I do not think, whether it is 92 or 93 will not significantly alter the nature of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 58 then is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might just, taking us through that map, indicate the respective positions of the various participants in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The map as composed was derived from information derived from Ministry of Defence information in the United Kingdom indicating areas of control. The area shaded in -- the area I am now indicating which to me is indicated in a kind of deep rose pink colour -- but I understand the colours appear differently on different monitors, so if people can acknowledge that whatever that colour is for them, that is the colour to which I am referring -- indicates territory under Serbian control. For most of the period we are talking about, the official designation for the force controlling this territory is the Vojska Republika Srpska, that is, the Army of the Serbian Republic, but, as we will, I believe, move to explain in further evidence, that army was de facto the remnants of the JNA. The area down here which for me is marked in blue represents Croatian forces, that is, the Bosnian Croatian HVO forces, but there were also elements of the Croatian army there. The area covered in green represents areas in which the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in control, or units associated with it in the case of places in eastern Bosnia. What the map shows overall is that a situation which, in terms of Serbian control of territories, changed very little from May 1992 through to the summer of 1995. It shows the degree to which the Serbian military and political forces took control of large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were the territories which were designated de facto as forming part of the Republika Srpska -- the Republika Srpska, as you recall from the constitutional documents we gave before, which regarded itself as being part of not Bosnia and Herzegovina but the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was one government in control of the whole of the area shown as Bosnian-Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that government one that was run from Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is certainly the case that the leadership based in Pale claimed responsibility for exercising government or tight authority over the whole of that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps that Exhibit might be returned?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One question about the map then. This would indicate areas of control in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the period May 1992 through the summer of 1995? Do I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the summer of 1995, that is correct, with -- there may be some small changes but, broadly, that would be the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that exhibit might be returned? I would ask you now, Dr. Gow, to look to the video monitor to watch the series being played which is part 5 of Exhibit 31, if your Honours please, of the video. Can part No. 5 of Exhibit 31 be now played? (Part 5 of Exhibit 31 was played). Dr. Gow -- just stopping there, please -- that was a very short segment. Can you tell us what it relates to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is again an extract taken from the series "Death of Yugoslavia" and it shows the leader of the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Radovan Karadzic, in the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The cutaway that you see while he is speaking is to Alija Itzebegovic, President at that time of Bosnia and Herzegovina and leader of the Muslim Party of Democratic Action. The Serbian Democratic Party leader is issuing a warning-come-threat in which he says, and this I believe was in March 1992, but I stand to be corrected, I may have misremembered that, in which he indicates that if the presidency and government in Bosnia and Herzegovina are to proceed to declare independence, to seek to have independent international personality, then the Muslim population would not be in a position to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does your Honours wish to see it again or was that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, it is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I hope this is not simple idle curiosity, but in your sheet of exhibits, if we subsequently are looking at these films, what are these times? Take 1, programme 3, time, I thought that was one hour 39 minutes. Is it one minute 39 seconds and then what are the fractions of a second?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If I can place it on the screen, I might explain it so that we can go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Because we will need to know when we play these over to ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand. If it can be put on the screen, I think I might be able to assist. There is a reference there right at the top of the page, your Honours, you will see that there is the title of the programme and it says that it is a five part series. The situation is that when this was copied for the purposes of providing it to our colleagues on the Defence, we put it on to two tapes. We put the whole series on to two tapes. Immediately underneath that, you can see tape 1 and it goes down and then it subsequently becomes tape 2. So what happens is that the Defence have two full tapes. If they need to look at the particular part of the programme being played in context, they can go precisely to the point in the tape and see it. Then they can see the side of it because they have the whole place provided. They are then given the time because on the bottom of the tape there is a time marker so it assists them in locating it. It is not really there in any sense so much for the court because the tape the court will get will only be the excerpts. We are not providing the tape with the whole five part series. It goes for many, many hours. It is a very, very long series. There were five programmes. We do indicate the reference to the programme is where it appears in the programme that was played on the BBC. So programme 2, programme 3 and so forth is where it appears. So if it were, your Honours, the first column -- in fact, it is the third column with writing in it, but the third column, which starts headed "Tape 1, programme 2" and then the numbers there is merely to assist the Defence. The part that your Honours may be assisted with at some subsequent stage, if you want to watch the tape, is where it says "Parts" because, if your Honours please, if you look at the tape when it is played, the one that will be tendered in evidence, it has a little number that comes up just before the sequence starts. That is corresponds with part 1, part 2, part 3, 4 and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Our copy is all on one roll, I understand, so it will be very simple for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yours is very simple.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will just play it and it will show consecutively as listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. So what your Honours are seeing is we are taking you to the parts, but it is all on the one tape. If you played it all, it would be no longer than, I would imagine, 10 minutes or something like that. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, what role, if any, did the paramilitary groups play in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paramilitary groups such as those to which reference was made yesterday organised by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and by Vojislav Seselj, were involved in the incidents in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the spring of 1992 at some of the places that I indicated on the map. Arkan was present in places such as Bijelina and Zvornik where his forces were used to go into the towns and to begin part of the process of taking control of those areas as part of the Serbian project and as part of the process of beginning to eliminate or expel those who would be non-loyal inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, it seems to the Defence that we are coming to a point where testimony is going to be given, at least we fear that it will be, on events that happened in approximately the time of the offences our client has been charged with. As far as the Defence is aware, the expert witness has no first hand knowledge of what actually happened at that time and at these places. So if it would come to questioning him about this, we would object because we think it proper that if this expert witness would give his opinion about the events that happened, that your Chamber first should hear witnesses or, at least, hear testimony from people who have seen and have heard and have been present during that time, and not start with hearing the expert opinions on these issues before having heard the evidence itself. I doubt a bit on what point exactly we should make this objection, but I think we either reach this point or we are coming quite near to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not entirely sure to what portion of the evidence the Defence are referring, your Honours, but no doubt they will take their objection in relation to any specific question I ask that they wish to object to. All I might say at this stage, and it is difficult to deal with it until we know precisely what the objection is and what it relates to, is that Dr. Gow has been, in our submission, qualified as an expert throughout his testimony up to now. He has referred to various sources that he has relied upon in order to express his opinion. He will do so, and continue to do so, throughout the balance of his testimony. In my submission, it is entirely appropriate and proper for an expert appropriately qualified, having regard to the source material that the expert has referred to and studied, to express an opinion about that. Just how much notice the court takes of the opinion in absence of any other evidence that may be tendered is a matter for the end of the day. It may be that on some matters there could be considerable evidence called of eyewitness testimony, and there may be in some areas not so much evidence. That is a question that will be addressed, no doubt, by the Defence in terms of how much weight your Honours should put on what Dr. Gow has said. In my submission, it is not a question of admissibility; it is entirely a question of weight. If Dr. Gow is accepted by the Tribunal as an expert, as I submit that he has been up-to-date, he has expressed his opinion, he is entitled to give that opinion. The Defence are perfectly entitled then to turn round and say that because there is nothing else other than Dr. Gow's opinion, or because of the basis upon which he expresses that opinion, your Honours should attribute little or indeed no weight to it. But that is for another time and another place. In my submission, there is nothing so far, and I apprehend that nothing Dr. Gow will say, will touch on the question of whether or not it should be admissible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I would like to point out that where the Prosecutor says that Dr. Gow has indicated his sources and has stressed that he is an expert in the field, I may remind you that one of the sources Dr. Gow mentioned is the witnesses of the Prosecutor. So, what we would like to prevent is that Dr. Gow's opinions as an expert represented here, although they may mainly be based on the statements of the Prosecutor's witnesses, and it is exactly at this moment that I object against this because, as far as we are aware, but we have not heard any details about that, as far as we are aware Dr. Gow has not been present in the area at the time we are approaching now, at least not in the places we are speaking of at this moment. I would strongly oppose arguing at the end of the day on what part of the opinions of Dr. Gow are without any factual basis, so just leave it as the Prosecutor suggests to a matter of arguing on the relevance of the statements, of the reliability, on the basis of it. I think your Chamber should not hear evidence that is at risk of being just a reproduction of the statements of the witnesses of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, here we are to discuss our Rules of Evidence, all 10 of them. The first objection that you raised, you indicated, Mr. Orie, that you considered that it was appropriate for the Defence to offer its witnesses first before hearing from Dr. Gow, that is persons who actually saw what happened, I thought that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know that that is necessary. It seems to me it is appropriate for the expert witness for the Prosecution to testify, assuming that proper foundation has been laid, before then. You will have your opportunity should you choose to offer witnesses, to speak contrary to what Dr. Gow testifies to. Of course, you will have your opportunity for cross-examination. So I do not know that we should wait for witnesses from the Defence before we hear from Dr. Gow. The problem with Dr. Gow's testimony, as I see it, really goes to the foundation, what he is basing his testimony on. As I recall, Dr. Gow said as he had indicated yesterday, and we saw parts, what did we see, parts 1 through 3 or 4 or parts 2 through 4 at least of Death of Yugoslavia or snippets of parts 2 and 3, just 2 and 3 I guess, we did not see any of part 4, just 2 and 3 and perhaps part 1. He made references or there were references made in the Death of Yugoslavia to paramilitary groups. But all of that, as I recall, Mr. Niemann, related to the conflict between Serbia and Croatia and had nothing to do with the presence of the paramilitary groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the area now that this witness is getting into talking about. Every single one of those snippets, except for I believe the report of the conference between Milosevic and President of Slovenia, had to do with the conflict between Serbia and Croatia. So that, for example, when we heard from Seselj when he spoke about paramilitary groups and when we heard from Bokan I guess and he spoke about Serbia supporting paramilitary groups, Bokan I guess was talking about Vukovar and that has nothing to do with the area the witness is now getting into. So it seems to me he is attempting to rely upon testimony that was related and restricted to the conflict between Croatia and Serbia to now say that there were paramilitary groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is really the problem where we are. That goes to foundation, it seems to me. You can handle it either by cross-examination or, if you want to, you can make the objection, but your objection that we should wait for witnesses I do not know that that is appropriate, Mr. Orie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: A misunderstanding, your Honour, because I did not only refer to witnesses of the Defence but as far as we can interpret the list of witnesses that are offered by the Prosecution that we think it appropriate to first hear those witnesses who may have first-hand knowledge of what happened and only afterwards hear Dr. Gow's expert upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask one question to elucidate? Your objection I understand is that you do not want Dr. Gow to give evidence based on evidence that is going to be given by Prosecution witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it is a problem. We do not know exactly what ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is it, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But that is the main issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It appears to the judges that to the extent Dr. Gow is an expert that he may base his opinion on evidence I suppose that is not yet in evidence. In other words, he is giving an expert opinion and the evidence upon which he is basing that opinion has not come into evidence. Now I do not know whether the Prosecutor is going to offer this evidence, the underlying documentation or support for Dr. Gow's opinion, but at this point he may give testimony as to his opinion. The question becomes what is he basing that on. So it seems to me you are entitled to ask him that. Mr. Niemann, I suppose in the interests of moving along, I would suggest that you ask Dr. Gow that. For example, yesterday when he gave us charts on the percentages of Serbs in the JNA force at different times, I asked him what it was based on. Judge Stephen asked him, "When you say 'Serbs' are you talking about Serbs from Serbia or Bosnian Serbs?" So, as long as it is made clear by Dr. Gow before he gives his opinion what he is basing his opinion on, then I think you will be in a good position, at least to cross-examine him or proceed how you wish at that point. We will let the testimony in and it really goes to the weight, but we suggest that you ask Dr. Gow to indicate what he is basing his opinion on before we Judges have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to make one additional observation. One of the reasons of the concern of the Defence is that the list of exhibits that has been presented to us is not at its end yet but almost at its end. So that is an additional reason for the Defence to fear that the sources might change in the questioning to come soon, because at least as we can see it looks as if there will be other sources to rely upon as far as the facts are concerned. That is the reason why. I appreciate very much that every subject to start with asking Dr. Gow what is the basis of his factual knowledge of what he will testify upon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. You understand the ruling. We are getting close to the end of the exhibits. We only have a few more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Which is a great relief!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, if you will do that, Mr. Niemann. Again it is a trial to the judges and much of it will go to weight, we will be able to separate out, but I think you have a legitimate concern of knowing on what he bases his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is just one matter, your Honour, I would like if I may to address, just something that fell from your Honour when you were discussing this. If we have given the impression in the presentation of our evidence that the excerpts of the tape of the Former Yugoslavia, exhibit 31, were in relation to the paramilitary, were limited only to paramilitary involved in the war in Croatia, then I regret that because I think perhaps, and I will ask Dr. Gow, we would say it goes further than that, that there was a general reference to the use of paramilitaries. We certainly would be putting it on that basis, that it is wider and it does apply to Bosnia as well, bearing in mind that the interviews took place at a much later stage. They were not contemporaneous with the war that was taking place between Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will take a look at it. I just remember what Seselj said. I remember what Bokan said and I thought that Bokan was talking about, if I am pronouncing the name correctly, Vukovar and Seselj again was talking, again after the fact but about at that point, at least in point in time it was my remembrance we were, even before the independence of Croatia. But that is just my recollection. You are certainly free to correct that, that is for sure, but at least we know about the parameters for the testimony of Dr. Gow as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Dr. Gow, if I might just take you to that question. Yesterday you were shown some excerpts of a tape which recorded conversations by a number of persons that you had identified as paramilitary leaders, including I believe Seselj and Bokan, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From your understanding of the subject matter that they were discussing, do you consider it was limited only to Croatia and the war between the former socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and Croatia, or do you believe it had a wider reference to events that occurred beyond that conflict leading into and including the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And if so on what do you base that opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reference made to the Dragoslav Bokan was with reference to Croatia. If you were to play the section designated part 2 again, I believe you would find in listening to Seselj that he talks not only about involvement in places in Croatia but he clearly states involvement with Bosnian Serbs. He says there were some Bosnian Serbs fighting but there were also armed forces, the JNA and special Police Forces from Serbia. If you care to play it again I think you will see that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now that is part 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is part 2.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would that be the first tape one interview with Seselj or which one so we can look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the material indicated as part 2 and it was towards the end of the material indicated as part 2. There were several references within part 2 on this schedule. If somebody could play maybe that could clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He makes references to paramilitary groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina and paramilitary groups receiving the backing of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be played, your Honour. Dr. Gow, I would ask if you could indicate where it is that you are referring to so the tape could be stopped at that point. (The tape was played).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You might want to stop this and pay attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, is this the part that is about now to follow, is this the part you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the part to which I was making reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be played on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, apart from the excerpt you have just seen there from the video, is there any other basis upon which you rely when you express or if you express an opinion about the involvement of the paramilitaries operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might remind your Honours and the Trial Chamber, when I began giving testimony I was asked on what basis I was giving evidence and at that stage I answered in the affirmative, that I was basing testimony on reading a variety of written sources, both official and non-official, both from the territories of the former Yugoslavia and from outside those territories. In addition to that I was basing the evidence on materials and on conversations with what I regard as knowledgeable people. I did not go into the detail of that, but the kinds of knowledge people to which I make reference are either those who have been in the area or those who have done particular work with regard to the area or those who are in positions working perhaps as officials of governments or international organisations to be able to express what I regard as credible opinions. I would base my judgments on that kind of information, and throughout that is what I have been attempting to do. As far as I will proceed in giving evidence, that is what I will continue in my attempt to do. With specific reference to the question of paramilitaries either in Croatia or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I see that there could be little problem in anybody discussing the presence of the those forces. There were open reports of the types of units described being involved in incidents in the places to which reference is made. I believe as evidence continues, one of the coming exhibits will also indicate the presence of these people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can only try on the basis of the -- I can only try on this basis to assist the court in what whatever way I can and as far as I can be expert in anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, in the last excerpt on the tape that we played there was a reference to Bosnia-Herzegovina or Bosnia I think it said, Bosnia. Do you know from what was said there to what part of Bosnia reference was being made by Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know to which particular part of Bosnia and Herzegovina Seselj was making reference. He was simply saying that there were Bosnian Serbs there but there were also his forces and forces from Serbia, and that the most significant forces were those from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would ask you now to look at the next document I show you. (Handed). Firstly, can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of the United Nations Security Council resolution 752 1992, dated 15 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who obtained the document, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 59?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 59 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, perhaps you could look at that document and, in particular -- well, perhaps show the first and second pages on the screen to start with. That is a resolution of what date? I think it is shown at the top there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date is 15th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Going particularly to paragraphs 3 and 4 on the second page of the document, do you rely on either of those paragraphs as support for your testimony in relation to the involvement of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. The two paragraphs indicated identify that units of the JNA, as well as units of the Croatian army, were present on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at this time. The Security Council is demanding that those units be withdrawn, unless they are placed under the control of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that Exhibit might be returned, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, does that resolution indicate what was the reason for the presence of the JNA? It indicates they are in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as, if we can take a look at it again, does it indicate they were engaged in a conflict with Bosnia-Herzegovina or perhaps as you indicated earlier they were on that soil using it as a jumping-off grouped, so to speak, for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be of assistance to your Honour if ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please, it went so quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- I can indicate that the Security Council considered the announcement on 4 May 1992 by the authorities in Belgrade on the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army personnel from Bosnia and Herzegovina other than those who were originally from the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where it says, "Having considered"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Having considered the announcement in Belgrade on 4 May 1992 described in paragraph 24 of the report of the Secretary General of 12 May 1992 concerning the withdrawal of Yugoslav People's Army personnel from republics other than Serbia and Montenegro and the renunciation of authority over those who remain."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means that on 4 May 1992 the authorities in Belgrade announced that the JNA would be withdrawn from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that that indicates that they were there. I guess my question is you testified earlier ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it indicates that the authorities in Belgrade on 4th May said that the forces would be withdrawn. The resolution on 15 May indicates that the forces are still present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is in paragraphs 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which is paragraphs 3 and 4 on the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand they were there, but I understand also from earlier testimony that you had indicated that they were in Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of a conflict with Croatia. My question is whether this resolution indicates that they were in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in conflict with the Bosnians or there as a part of their conflict with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall if the resolution makes comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you go to the first part of the resolution you see the third paragraph, the third paragraph "Deeply concerned"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third paragraph does indicate the concern of the Security Council for the depressingly violent situation, particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Further down it notes the tragic incident on 4th May 1992 in which a member of the European Community Monitor Mission was killed. The resolution -- I will quickly check -- if I can take your Honour back to paragraph 3, you will see, I think you can take it from the demand of the Security Council that outside elements, including units of the Yugoslav People's Army, ceased immediately that interference, that the Security Council regarded the presence of the Yugoslav People's Army units, and the Croatian army units possibly, as being interference in the internal affairs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It does not state specifically how the Security Council regarded the purpose of that interference.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30 please. (1.05 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I think Dr. Gow is coming in. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just prior to the adjournment for lunch, you were looking for us at the United Nations Security Council resolution 752, which is dated 15th May 1992, and has become Exhibit 59. Dr. Gow, can you tell us what the state of the conflict was in Croatia at the time of the passing of the adopting of this resolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There had been a cease fire in the conflict in Croatia signed on 2nd January 1992 under the auspices of the European Community and the United Nations. That was the cease fire between the government of Croatia and its forces, the JNA and Serbian, local Serbian forces in Croatia. Therefore, in a formal sense, the conflict in Croatia was not carrying on, although there were repeated violations of that cease fire agreement which were reported, but these were small but they were on a regular basis. I think it is important to note that much of what I have been saying in testimony was, in the first instance, with relation to Croatia, but then has also been in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina and that much of the evidence that I have been trying to give is indicating the nature of the war. I think it may be a mistake that because there are two theatres of war, one in Croatia and one in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to treat, to think of it as two separate questions. The central element in all of this is the project to create the set of territories involving the linked Serbian units between Serbia, through the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Serbia in Croatia. So, therefore, all of this activity is connected. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina is one aspect. In a way, it is rather like regarding the war -- during the Second World War regarding Germany's eastern front war with the Soviet Union as being a separate war from its western front campaign with the western allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, was Security Council resolution 752 of 15th May 1992 complied with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Security Council react to the noncompliance with resolution 752?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did. It met and it issued a further Security Council resolution which was 757.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the document I now show you? (Handed) Is this Security Council resolution 757?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a copy of Security Council resolution 757, dated 30 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 60 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, I think if we could go to the second page of the resolution, to the heading "Deploring":

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the section indicated beginning "Deploring", the Security Council indicates that there has not been compliance with the demands made in resolution 752. Among those items to which reference was made in 752, it goes on to note that, to reaffirm the involvement, the point about the involvement of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that exhibit be returned to the Registrar? I would now ask for part 6 of Exhibit 31, the video, be now played, please? Dr. Gow, I just ask you to watch it first and then we will come back to it, if we may. (Part 6 of Exhibit 31 was played) Dr. Gow, who is the gentleman that has been interviewed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Borisav Jovic who had been the representative of President Milosevic of the Republic of Serbia to the collective state presidency of the SFRY in its final phase. President Jovic -- sorry, Mr. Jovic, in this instance, is discussing the decision to take measures with regard to the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those measures involved preparations for moving people of Bosnian-Serb origin within the JNA into Bosnia and Herzegovina so they would be deployed there and rotating those as many as possible who were not from Bosnia and Herzegovina to the territories of Serbia and Montenegro. What President Jovic -- forgive me; I do not know why I keep saying that -- what Mr. Jovic is saying is that they decided that it was clear that if the JNA remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina as the JNA, it would be regarded by the outside world as an aggressor, that is, in fulfilling its role in the project I identified earlier with reference particularly to the book by General Kadijevic and, therefore, what they would do would be to attempt to blur the issue and to deceive the outside world to some extent. That is to say, that the JNA would be withdrawn, but at the same time de facto the JNA would be divided. So, those people who were not citizens -- those people in the JNA who would be citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina because they were born there would remain with JNA units in Bosnia and would be transformed into the Army of the Serbian Republic. But because the Army of the Serbian Republic and the Republika Srpska itself would not have resources for such an army, Belgrade would continue to pay for and to provide officers for an armed force of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he makes reference ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I might say -- this is similar in a way to the tactic which General Kadijevic described with reference to Croatia -- I mentioned this in testimony yesterday -- the idea that you cannot make it clear to the international community what it is that you are doing; you have to, you say that you are doing one thing because you do not want to put yourself in a situation where you might face particular actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say there was an attempt to deceive the international community of what was happening, is that your understanding of what he means when he uses the term "pulling a fast one"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The translation on the screen used the term "pulling a fast one". He is attempting, indeed, to indicate the way in which they intended that they would remove any clear sense that it was the JNA controlled by Belgrade which was operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of this project for creating the set of states. I should also point out that the decision to do this was announced on 4th May 1992, at which point it was indicated that they intended the process of withdrawal, what they call the withdrawal of the JNA, that is, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- sorry, citizens of Serbia and Montenegro would -- that the process announced on May 4 would be complete by May 19, and that that process was the withdrawal of citizens of -- the withdrawal of the JNA which, in effect, meant the withdrawal of citizens of Serbia and Montenegro and some of the equipment of the JNA. The bulk of the equipment of the JNA was left with the forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, this was a concern in Belgrade, was it not, that arose because the Security Council by this stage had already passed a resolution making demands with respect to the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a concern because it was already clear that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was being discussed in the international arena in a way which might lead to the imposition of a sanctions regime or other action against Serbia and Montenegro. resolution 752 of May 15 indicated this concern for the presence of the JNA. resolution 757 of May 30 took the measure of applying economic, political sanctions against Serbia and Montenegro because it was regarded as being responsible for the continuing presence of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was indicated in resolution 752 -- sorry, in resolution 757.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do your Honours need to see that again?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do your Honours wish to see the tape played again or is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, when the JNA divided itself, what were the respective titles given to the two halves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After May 19, when the formal date for withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina had been -- after the date for which formal withdrawal had been designated, May 19, the old, what was left of the old JNA was, effectively, divided. It was divided into the army of the Serbian Republic, the Vojska Republika Srpska, the VRS, and the Vojska Jugoslavije, the Army of Yugoslavia, that is, of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your opinion, did this division of the JNA amount to a genuine withdrawal of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was clear that the decision to withdraw the JNA in this was not a decision so much to withdraw the JNA as to avoid, or attempt to avoid, some of the political assessments which would be made in the international arena and which, indeed, were made nonetheless. The attempt, the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and, indeed, in Croatia after the withdrawal of JNA forces in the same manner from Croatia in the first part of 1992, that is, from the parts of Croatia occupied and controlled by Serbian forces, where weaponry and elements were left behind for the local Serbian forces, the same thing happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The aim of this, as I was saying, was to give the impression that it was a matter purely internal to Bosnia and Herzegovina, although it is significant that the forces provided as a result of this split in the JNA left -- were part of the single project I identified for connecting the states, the project identified in General Kadijevic's book, and that this action was clearly distinct from the action taken by the JNA in withdrawing from Slovenia, from non-Serbian controlled territories in Croatia and from the Republic of Macedonia. In all those cases, the JNA withdrew all its equipment and in many cases destroyed facilities and things which would be left behind which might be of benefit. So, in taking this action, Belgrade was giving a very clear and substantial -- taking a very clear and substantial position on the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the degree to which assistance was being given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the next document I show you, please? (Handed). What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a copy of a report of the Secretary General of the United Nations dated 3rd December 1992, and the copy is taken from the Cambridge International Documents series.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 61 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, just looking at this document and in terms of what you have just been discussing in your testimony, can you tell us the significance of this report by the Secretary General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance of the report is that following on from the references I have made to resolutions 752 and 757 regarding the presence of the forces of neighbouring countries in Bosnia and Herzegovina interfering in the independence and territorial integrity of that state, the report from the end of 1992, that is, several months after the Security Council resolutions to which I made reference, indicates the continuing presence of the Croatian Army and reports the alleged presence of the Yugoslav People's Army -- sorry, the continued presence of the Yugoslav Army, by this time the VJ, the Vojska Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you draw our attention, please, to those references?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will note the reference to the question of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the elements of the JNA as per the earlier resolutions. If you move down through, if we can move down through it, you will see that the Secretary General is continuing through UNPROFOR to receive credible reports of extensive involvement of forces of the Croatian Army, and also that, allegedly, the Bosnian Serb forces, that is, the VRS, the part of the JNA which was left active in Bosnia and Herzegovina, continues to receive assistance from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. These are all supported by journalistic accounts of other things. The greater emphasis on the presence of the Croatian Army is because the Croatian Army was operating in areas where Spanish, French and British troops with UNPROFOR were present and were able to give clear and authoritative accounts. The reports for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia assistance are described as "allegedly" because they cannot be given on the same basis, but they are, nonetheless, broadly regarded as being credible by those who were there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that exhibit be returned and, Dr. Gow, I would like to take you back, if I may, to Dr. Kadijevic's book, firstly, Exhibit 30, if that could be given to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still have it; it was never taken away before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. It is still with the witness. Page 65. It may not be that page. Would you look at page 80?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was finding it difficult to see anything of relevance on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you can move up, I can see immediately that page 80 looks far more relevant. I draw your attention to the paragraph I am indicating now. You will see General Kadijevic, in effect, confirming what I was saying before. I will read the quote, read aloud the extract which is in italics: "The units and headquarters of the JNA formed the backbone of the Army of the Serb Republic, complete with weaponry and equipment. That Army, with the full support of the Serb people, which is required in any modern war, protected the Serb people and created the military conditions for an adequate political solution", that is one which would achieve the creation of these republics, Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the Republic of Serbian Krajina which, as far as international circumstances would permit, would be joined with Federal Yugoslavia and which, according to their constitutions, regarded themselves as constituting part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but not of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On page 88, perhaps, if you could look at that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, General Kadijevic is confirming the point that it was the JNA which was carrying out these operations in conjunction and co-operation with Serbian irregular forces, first of all, in his terms, to liberate Serbian Krajina, but also in Bosnia and Herzegovina the JNA, later the Army of the Republic of Srpska, which the JNA put on its feet, helped to liberate Serb territory, that is, to create effective Serbian control of the territories which were indicated on one of the maps I showed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be removed from the screen? Had the JNA prepared themselves for this division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the period leading up to the division of the JNA into the VRS and the VJ, as I think I already said, to be clear, members of the Army who were from Bosnia and Herzegovina were being moved into Bosnia and Herzegovina while, as far as possible, those who were citizens of Serbia and Montenegro were being withdrawn from Bosnia and Herzegovina. After May 19 1992, many of those, although for some time after that many were to remain, for the most part those who were citizens of Serbia and Montenegro were withdrawn, although not within the time frame that was indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Belgrade though continue to support the Serb forces in Bosnia after May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did, not only with the supply of -- with logistics assistance and the supply of material, but also at certain periods through the presence of the armed forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at the document I now show you? Can you tell me what the document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is an extract from the Summary of World Broadcasts, Eastern European series. The Summary of World Broadcasts is produced by the BBC monitoring service at Caversham in the United Kingdom. This particular extract refers to the speech given by Slobodan Milosevic, President of Serbia, to the Assembly of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina on, I think, 11 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you consider it as a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I consider it to be a reliable source, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 62 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Firstly, this is a broadcast on 11 May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you take us to any particular part of that exhibit that you wish to refer in relation to your testimony concerning the involvement of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will take you through the two pages of the document, if I may? First of all, the report on the left-hand side indicates the address given by -- the address was given by Slobodan Milosevic to the Assembly of the Bosnian Serbs. If I can move to the right-hand page, apart from the first paragraph, the remainder is text of a statement given by Slobodan Milosevic to Tanjug. Tanjug is the Yugoslav state press agency. If you begin to move through, he makes several references that during the past two years the Republic of Serbia assisting Serbs outside Serbia and the difficulties of the situation in which this has put the Republic of Serbia. "Because of its solidarity with assistance to the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia is subjected to brutal international sanctions". That is the sanctions regime first imposed by resolutions 757, although shortly after this those measures were to be strengthened by a further Security Council resolution. "Clearly, we were aware we would face these difficulties when deciding to provide assistance to Serbs who were at war. Now conditions for peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina have been created", and, therefore, he goes on to suggest that the war should be stopped. If you move through, if you keep moving through and maybe move on to the next page, again he makes reference, "Serbia has lent a great, great deal of assistance to the Serbs in Bosnia and owing to that assistance they", that is the Bosnian Serbs, "have achieved most of what they wanted". At this point he is indicating Serbia should begin to take care of itself and, therefore, he is urging, he has been urging the Bosnian Serbs (and this is in the address he gave at Pale) to accept proposals for a settlement at that time, that is, that the settlement in question was the one known as the Vance Owen plan. I think that is probably enough for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, apart from the matters that you have already referred to, which you cite, as examples of Belgrade's continued involvement in the Bosnian war after May 1992, are there any other examples that you know of of such continued involvement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are. Belgrade on a number of occasions was noted to have had forces deployed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In several cases, these were not necessarily always large units, but there were cases during 1993 and 94 where units of the VJ were involved in operations with regard to Bosnia. Elements of the 63rd Airborne Division were involved -- Airborne Brigade -- were involved near Sarajevo. Elements of the Nis and Uzice corps were involved in a number of locations in eastern and southern Bosnia. There were reports of elements of the Novi Sad corps being involved during 1992 and after in parts of eastern Bosnia, particularly in the areas around Zvornik, Bijeljina, and activity continued into 1994 where there was evidence of joint air activity between elements of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, the Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look please, at the next document that you are shown? (Handed). What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a further extract from the Trifunovska "Yugoslavia Through Documents" volume. This particular extract relates to a letter from the President of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the President of the Security Council concerning a decision by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to proclaim a state of war. The date of that letter is 22 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 63?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 63 is admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): In relation to this question of the involvement of the Yugoslav Army, can you take us to the specific reference for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I would emphasise the significance of this document is that the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as wanting to make a formal political and legal declaration of a state of war. If I can move to the second page -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Before you do, the state of war is not proclaimed with any other particular specified country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The proclamation of the state of war is made with reference -- in making the proclamation of the state of war reference is made to Security Council resolution 752 and, therefore, I think could be taken as by being reference to that resolution is also with reference to the presence of the forces of neighbouring countries on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At that time, I am not quite clear of the status of the enemy, it would be the new Federation of Serbia and Montenegro, or the remnants of the old Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the case of Belgrade forces deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would be forces of the newly declared Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro. That was declared on 27th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the date I wanted, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the second page, could you .....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the second page in the letter, the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina continues, indicates, that the Yugoslav Air Force, in particular, he advised as being involved in bombing campaigns, bombing operations, at Gorazde and Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those two towns are in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think there is further reference further down the page, is there, it is not the declaration of war but -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He goes on to identify the action in the eyes of Bosnia and Herzegovina as being an act of aggression and indicates that artillery and airfields in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Serbia and Montenegro have been used as part of this campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Finally, I just point out that he goes on to say beyond that in his request, in view of that fact, Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding itself as subject to an act of aggression by the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro and the Yugoslav Army as well as the internal elements of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is that a reference to, the terrorists of the Serbian democratic party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are the local Serbian forces of the, Serbian irregular forces of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, led by Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that Exhibit might be exhibited? Would you now look at the document I show you? (Handed) What is that a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of the area around Gorazde in south-eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is a map which indicates certain movements of military forces in March and April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who prepared the map, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor at my direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 64 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you look at that map and can you explain for us the significance of the markings that appear there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outer set of markings, the broken line I am running along now, indicates roughly the area around Gorazde declared as a safe area under the auspices of the United Nations and, for the most part, under Bosnian/Muslim control. The red line indicates the front line to which Bosnian, Serbian and other forces moved in the course of April 1994. The green lines indicate the lines of attack taken, taken in order to carry out that attack. There should be a marking, maybe this is the marking here, yes -- no, there should be a marking somewhere here which indicates the border between Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. If I could add -- if I could see with my own eyes first of all, I might be able to identify it because it does not seem to come through very clearly. It still does not come through very clearly. I will just have to indicate that the border, for the purposes of what I have to say, the presence of the border between Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina which is somewhere there, although I stand to be corrected by an accurate border being indicated, the significance of this is that in the operations of Gorazde in April 1994 elements of special units from the Nis corps of the Vojska Jugoslavije and units of the Uzice corps were reported to have been involved. The those reports of involvement also are supplemented by a deduction from the line of attack, which is that Serbia and Montenegro has to have been giving assistance in order for this attack to have taken place because the gathering point at Cajnice in northern Montenegro is on the point of the -- access to the gathering point is only via the road across the border. Forces gathering there could not have come from anywhere else but Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at the next document that I show you? In connection with that particular -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, and I reserve a lack of certainty on this, I think I have identified the problem in the preparation of map, and that the border is here and runs across there and that this is the route which forces to have come to Cajnice for the attack would have to have taken from the Republic of Montenegro which lies just off the edge of this map now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to the attack on Gorazde, what is the document that I have now shown you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a paper headed, titled "The truth about Gorazde" dated May 4, 1994. It is on headed paper from the Task Force on Terrorism and Unconventional Warfare of the House Republican Research Committee of the US House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you consider that to be a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I considered it to be a reliable source for the purposes of this evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 65 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, I think, if you could place page 9, you might have a look at it first. Perhaps you might refer to the section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In particular, I would draw your attention to the paragraph I am now indicating in which the report identifies, the report concerned with the attack on Gorazde, identifies components of the Uzice corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Uzice corps is based at Ujzice in south western Serbia and special forces from the Nis area, that is, Nis is again within the 3rd military district of the Vojska Jugoslavije in southern Serbia. Maybe I would be permitted to explain something about the character of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is significant that the bulk of the document is more concerned with identifying in what it describes about the truth about Gorazde in describing the activities of Bosnian government army and Muslim units in the area around Gorazde. It was compiled, obviously, by people who were well informed, but who did not necessarily, I think, know where Nis and Uzice were. It is my judgment that it was prepared in that context to persuade people in Congress in the US, possibly and probably -- I stress this is speculation and only interpretation from the material that is there -- that in the complex situation such as the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina that the bulk of responsibility for the events of Gorazde lay with the Bosnian government army. The inclusion of the references to Nis and Uzice, I think, I would probably interpret as being based on reliable information, but on a failure to understand where Nis and Uzice are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps that document might be returned? Dr. Gow, dealing with the pattern of the spring 1992 attacks in Bosnia, do you, in your opinion, consider that the spring offensive was a planned operation by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operations in the spring of 1992 were planned and co-ordinated actions involving elements of the JNA, local Serbian Territorial Defence units and paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to that, would you look now, please, at the document that you are shown? (Handed) Would you look at those pages that are now given to you? What are they? While you are dealing with that, could you just refer, please, to the number that appears on the top of each one when you describe each one? When you describe each one, can you tell us in reference to the number that appears in the top -- you see 2/15, 2/16 and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Map 2/15 indicates certain Yugoslav Army air bases in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Map 2/16 is a map indicating selected infrastructure resources in parts of the former Yugoslavia. Map 2/17 is a selected indication of industry in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Finally, map 2/18 is a map showing certain towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the complete layout of the local government, local government areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those local government areas are sometimes referred to as Opstinas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are the Opstina in Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender those, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Exhibit 66?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 66 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, looking at these maps, can you demonstrate for us by reference to them the nature of the spring attacks? When you are referring to them progressively, would you make reference to the number that appears at the top so it can be indicated for the record which number you are referring to at any given time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dealing with map 2/15 at the moment, indicating the air bases in Bosnia and Herzegovina, broadly speaking, the areas which were involved in the initial campaign also included, or attempted to include, these air bases. The air base at Tuzla was not occupied by the JNA and its associates at that time. The JNA destroyed the facilities at the air base at Bihac. As it pulled out, it left -- it continued to use the air bases around Banja Luka and after the division of the JNA ostensibly in May 1992, air force units were left to operate from Banja Luka with the VRS. The airport at Sarajevo was controlled by the Serbs throughout the conflict until the point in 1992 where, with their agreement, the United Nations formally took control of running it, and French units of the UNPROFOR from the summer of 1992 onwards formally controlled the airport, although only with Serbian agreement. This map of selected infrastructure through parts of Yugoslavia again indicates a set of oil pipelines and gas pipelines and so forth which run broadly along the axes of the war in Croatia and the war in Bosnia running down through parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It may well be that part of the activity of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was to secure control of areas in which these facilities and so forth were present as well as of the main communications axes. That map was 2/16. Map 2/17 indicating industry in Bosnia and Herzegovina; again you will see the broad area of which the Serbian forces took control is also, broadly, the area in which particular assets can be identified.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I cannot determine on the map, are they diagrams of the industry, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The symbols represent different aspects of industry. This little symbol here represents metallurgy, for example, and this represents chemical industry. The final map, 2/18, is simply for reference to the particular Opstina throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, should it be of use to the court, in seeing where particular situations might have occurred and where they relate to the territories which claimed as part of the Serbian autonomous provinces and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can confirm that the final map was 2/18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, would you look at this document that is shown to you? (Handed) What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is Annex III(A) on special forces of the final report of the United Nations Commission of Experts established pursuant to Security Council resolution 780, 1992. The date on the document which has the reference S/1994/674/ Annex III(A) is 27 May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 67 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, what support do you seek to obtain from this document in terms of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document indicates ways in which paramilitary groups and the JNA operated in parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of the campaign being undertaken in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there a specific reference to that on page 166?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just point out, first of all, that the report, as well as indicating the elements of the Serbian campaign with which my evidence is primarily concerned, also indicates the activity of some Croatian and Muslim paramilitary groups within Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that the bulk of the sections to which I made reference first of all deal with what is described as Zvornik County, that is Zvornik Opstina, and indicates the presence, first of all, of forces loyal to Vojislav Seselj. If I might take the opportunity to indicate with reference to evidence given this morning, when we saw the individual evidence of Seselj talking about involvement in Bosnia, I took the liberty on checking on this and he was speaking specifically with reference to the town of Zvornik in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The document goes on to detail the presence, not only of Seselj paramilitary forces, but also of those of the Serbian volunteer guard of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that might be returned? Would you look at this document that is shown to you? What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Annex IV to the same document to which I just made reference, that is, the Security Council document S/1994/674, Annex IV, dated 22nd May 1994; again part of the final report of the United Nations Commission of Experts. The Annex is titled "The Policy of Ethnic Cleansing".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 68 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Gow, what part of this document do you seek to rely on for the purposes of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can go through, first of all, again beginning with the reference to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Zvornik, elements of the JNA are identified from the 1st military district and from the 2nd military district being involved in the area in preparations, moving out and taking positions around Zvornik in the period before the onset of major armed hostilities and before the formal recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and then moving through to identify particular units which were involved in the early phases of the armed conflict. The document also goes on to identify the presence of some of the paramilitary groups to which we have already made reference in the course of my giving testimony. Specifically here we can see reference to paramilitary units with the exception of those controlled by Arkan which were judged to be identified as being under the authority of JNA officers. We can move further through the document, you will see `various references to the paramilitary groups and to their use of JNA uniforms and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that be returned? Dr. Gow, I would now ask you to watch a very short video sequence and then after watching it I will ask you some questions in relation to it. Your Honours, I am referring to 69 in the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 69?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 69 will be admitted. (The video was played) Dr. Gow, are you aware of who prepared this? Firstly, tell me what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the opening sequence from a special edition of the programme entitled "The Cook Report" and it is produced by Central Television in Birmingham, in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any involvement in the preparation of this series?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had some involvement acting as a consultant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could part No. 1 of the series be played, please, part No. 1 of Exhibit 69. (Part No. 1 of Exhibit 69 was played) Dr. Gow, I think it is obvious from the clip that that was Arkan that was shown there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us are you aware of the time frame that that related to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give a specific time frame for the period in which that recording was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know to what area or what theatre of the war it related to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was made as a video made by Arkan himself, I do not think we can be clear whether he was referring to part of the war in Croatia or part of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what political measures were taken by the Serbs concurrent with the military activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As well as the types of military, paramilitary operation to which I have made reference, the Serbian forces had also been engaged in a series of political preparations for taking control in areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina further to the declarations of the Serbian autonomous provinces. In particular, certainly from the end of 1991 onwards, the Serbian Democratic Party in conjunction with security service centres was preparing to take control in certain areas and making the provision for shadow secret governments which would take up their role in office at a designated point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would now ask you to look at the document I show you. (Handed) What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document is a document of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its principal committee or chief committee. It is marked "Strictly confidential". This is example or copy No., I think, 96. It is dated 19th December 1991. It is on a document on the organisation and activity of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and emergency circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where this document was obtained from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the document was obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I use it in evidence on the basis that I understand it has been assessed by qualified experts from governments which are members of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Therefore, do you consider it to be a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of those assessments, I would consider it to be reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 70 will be admitted. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): In relation to the testimony you have just given, do you find that this document provides some support for your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it does; the document indicates preparations for the creation of these para governmental structures through the establishment of what are called crisis headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you show us that, please, by placing it on the overhead projector specifically to the .....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document indicates tasks and measures to be carried out and divides those by those people involved in the planning for the creation of these governmental forms and identifies two categories for the planning; one is in areas in which the Serbian people form the majority, described as option (A), and one for areas in which Serbian people are not in the majority, described as option (B). If I could move on? The remainder of the document deals with the two options and takes them through stages.
